{{short description|Theorem about diagonalizing matrices}}
{{More footnotes needed|date=September 2024}}
In the context of [[linear algebra]] and [[symplectic geometry]], the '''Williamson theorem''' concerns the diagonalization of [[Definite matrix|positive definite matrices]] through [[Symplectic matrix|symplectic matrices]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Williamson |first=John |date=1936 |title=On the Algebraic Problem Concerning the Normal Forms of Linear Dynamical Systems |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2371062 |journal=American Journal of Mathematics |volume=58 |issue=1 |pages=141–163 |doi=10.2307/2371062 |jstor=2371062 |issn=0002-9327|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Nicacio |first=F. |date=2021-12-01 |title=Williamson theorem in classical, quantum, and statistical physics |journal=American Journal of Physics |volume=89 |issue=12 |pages=1139–1151 |doi=10.1119/10.0005944 |issn=0002-9505|arxiv=2106.11965 |bibcode=2021AmJPh..89.1139N }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Yusofsani |first=Mohammad |date=25 November 2018 |title=Symplectic Geometry and Wiliamson's Theorem |url=https://math.arizona.edu/~rsims/ma541/Seye_lec.pdf |access-date=25 November 2018}}</ref>

More precisely, given a strictly positive-definite <math>2n\times 2n</math> Hermitian real matrix <math>M\in\mathbb{R}^{2n\times 2n}</math>, the theorem ensures the existence of a real symplectic matrix <math>S\in\mathbf{Sp}(2n,\mathbb{R})</math>, and a diagonal positive real matrix <math>D\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}</math>, such that <math display="block">SMS^T = I_2\otimes D \equiv D\oplus D,</math>where <math>I_2</math> denotes the 2x2 [[identity matrix]].

== Proof ==
The derivation of the result hinges on a few basic observations:

# The real matrix <math>M^{-1/2} (J\otimes I_n) M^{-1/2}</math>, with <math>J\equiv\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}</math>, is well-defined and skew-symmetric.
# For any invertible skew-symmetric real matrix <math>A\in\mathbb{R}^{2n\times 2n}</math>, there is <math>O\in\mathbf{O}(2n)</math> such that <math>OAO^T= J\otimes \Lambda</math>, where  <math>\Lambda</math> a real positive-definite [[diagonal matrix]] containing the [[singular value]]s of <math>A</math>.
# For ''any'' orthogonal <math>O\in\mathbf O(2n)</math>, the matrix <math>S= \left(I_2\otimes\sqrt D\right)O M^{-1/2}</math> is such that <math>SMS^T=I_2\otimes D</math>.
# If <math>O\in\mathbf O(2n)</math> diagonalizes <math>M^{-1/2} (J\otimes I_n) M^{-1/2}</math>, meaning it satisfies <math display="block">OM^{-1/2} (J\otimes I_n) M^{-1/2}O^T=J\otimes\Lambda, </math>then <math>S= \left(I_2\otimes\sqrt D\right)O M^{-1/2}</math> is such that <math display="block">S(J\otimes I_n)S^T=J\otimes (D\Lambda) .</math>Therefore, taking <math>D=\Lambda^{-1}</math>, the matrix <math>S</math> is also a symplectic matrix, satisfying <math>S(J\otimes I_n)S^T=J\otimes I_n</math>.
